Name: Mission Inn
Description: Beginning with the Mission Inn’s original Mission-style wing in 1903, owner Frank A. Miller transformed a modest family hotel into an extraordinary architectural complex over the next three decades. Architects Arthur B. Benton, Myron Hunt, G. Stanley Wilson and Peter J. Weber contributed to its successive additions, combining Mission Revival, Spanish, Mediterranean and other influences with art and architectural fragments collected from around the world. The Mission Inn is also a National Historic Landmark and one of Riverside’s defining historic places.

Name: Riverside County Courthouse
Description: Completed in the early twentieth century as Riverside County’s first permanent courthouse, this monumental Beaux-Arts building was designed by architect Franklin P. Burnham. Its classically composed façade, Ionic columns and sculptural ornament were inspired by the Grand Palais built for the 1900 Paris Exposition. The courthouse reflects Riverside’s rapid growth and rising civic ambitions following the creation of Riverside County in 1893.

Name: Universalist-Unitarian Church
Description: Built in 1891–92 for Riverside’s Universalist congregation, this picturesque Gothic Revival church was designed by architect A. C. Willard. Constructed of brick faced with red Arizona sandstone, it features a prominent corner tower, steeply pitched roofs and stained-glass windows recalling a medieval English parish church. It is one of downtown Riverside’s most distinctive surviving nineteenth-century religious buildings.

Name: Magnolia Presbyterian Church
Description: Built in 1881 for the First Presbyterian Church of Arlington, this Gothic Revival church was designed and constructed by architect A. W. Boggs. Its simple form and pointed-arch detailing reflect the small agricultural community that developed around Arlington before its incorporation into Riverside. It is the oldest surviving church building in the city.

Name: Catherine Bettner House (Heritage House)
Description: Built in 1891–92 for Catherine Bettner, widow of citrus grower James Bettner, Heritage House is one of Riverside’s finest surviving Queen Anne residences. Designed by Los Angeles architect John A. Walls, the elaborate house reflects the prosperity generated by Riverside’s booming citrus industry during the late nineteenth century. Now operated by the Museum of Riverside, it preserves both the architecture and domestic setting of Riverside’s citrus-era elite.

Name: First Congregational Church
Description: Designed by noted architect Myron Hunt and constructed in 1912–13, First Congregational Church is an important early expression of Spanish Colonial Revival architecture in California. Its massive masonry walls, arcades, exposed timber roof and richly ornamented Churrigueresque tower give the church a commanding presence at Mission Inn Avenue and Lemon Street. Dedicated in January 1914, it predates the widespread popularity of the style following the 1915 Panama-California Exposition.

Name: First Church of Christ, Scientist
Description: Completed in 1900, the First Church of Christ, Scientist is one of architect Arthur B. Benton’s important early Riverside commissions and an influential example of the emerging Mission Revival style. Its use of mission-inspired forms helped establish an architectural vocabulary that would soon become closely identified with Riverside and Southern California. The building is also listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

Name: Victoria Avenue
Description: Planned in 1892 as the principal boulevard through Matthew Gage’s Arlington Heights development, Victoria Avenue is one of Riverside’s most important historic cultural landscapes. Landscape designer Franz P. Hosp supervised its early planting, establishing the palms, eucalyptus and ornamental vegetation that gave the divided avenue its distinctive park-like character. Extending for miles through former citrus lands, Victoria Avenue embodies Riverside’s citrus-era development, landscape planning and civic identity.

Name: San Pedro, Los Angeles & Salt Lake Railroad Depot (Union Pacific Depot)
Description: Built in 1904 for the San Pedro, Los Angeles & Salt Lake Railroad, this Mission Revival depot reflects the importance of rail transportation to Riverside’s early twentieth-century growth and citrus economy. The railroad became part of the Union Pacific system in 1921, and the depot remained in passenger service until 1971. Its broad arches, stucco walls and tile roof made the building a prominent architectural gateway to the city.

Name: Fairmount Park Bandshell
Description: Designed by architect Arthur B. Benton and completed in 1920, the Fairmount Park Bandshell was created as a permanent setting for Riverside’s popular public concerts. Its Mission-inspired tile roof and fieldstone construction harmonize with the park landscape and with Benton’s other Riverside work. The bandshell was dedicated before an audience of approximately 6,000 on September 26, 1920, and became an enduring center of civic entertainment in Fairmount Park.

Name: Former U.S. Post Office and Federal Building (Museum of Riverside)
Description: Built between 1912 and 1914 as Riverside’s U.S. Post Office and federal building, this Italian Renaissance Revival structure later housed the Riverside Police Department before becoming the permanent home of the city museum. The Museum gradually expanded from space in the basement to occupy the entire building by 1966. Its substantial civic architecture reflects Riverside’s growth and importance as a regional center in the early twentieth century.

Name: S. C. Evans Residence
Description: Built about 1874 for Samuel C. Evans, president of the Riverside Land and Irrigating Company, this early adobe residence is attributed to architect W. R. Norton. Constructed largely from local natural materials, the house is a rare survivor of Riverside’s first years of development and represents a building tradition that largely disappeared as the young colony prospered and more permanent frame and masonry residences replaced adobe construction.

Name: “Castillo Isabella” Benedict Castle (Teen Challenge)
Description: Designed by Riverside architect Henry L. A. Jekel for Charles W. Benedict, this imposing residence was constructed in stages between 1921 and 1931. Jekel combined Spanish and Mediterranean forms with pronounced Moorish influences, creating one of Riverside’s most distinctive examples of romantic revival architecture. Conceived as a luxurious private residence, the castle later became associated with Teen Challenge and remains one of Jekel’s best-known works.

Name: Buena Vista Drive & Former St. Francis Fountain Gateway (Carlson Bark Park)
Description: This linear landmark preserves remnants of Riverside’s historic western gateway along the former approach to the Santa Ana River bridge at the foot of Mount Rubidoux. Surviving features include the Mission Revival bridge towers, Raincross streetlights and balustrades, stone retaining walls and walkways, Buena Vista Bridge, Carlson Park and the remains of the St. Francis water feature. Together they reflect several decades of civic improvement and the deliberate creation of a picturesque entrance to Riverside.

Name: Parent Navel Orange Tree
Description: One of the original Washington navel orange trees sent to Riverside in 1873, this tree helped launch the citrus industry that transformed the city and much of Southern California. Eliza and Luther Tibbets successfully cultivated the new variety, whose seedless, easily peeled fruit proved exceptionally well suited to the region. Budwood from their trees was widely propagated, making Riverside the center of a vast commercial citrus industry. The surviving tree is both Riverside City Landmark No. 15 and California Historical Landmark No. 20.

Name: Former Sherman Institute Administration Building (Sherman Indian Museum)
Description: Built in 1901 as the administration building of the Sherman Institute, this Mission Revival structure is the principal surviving building from the school’s original campus of more than thirty buildings. The federal boarding school was established to educate Native American students from California and throughout the West as part of a national assimilation program that sought to separate Indigenous children from their languages, families and cultures. Today the building houses the Sherman Indian Museum and documents the history and experiences of the school and its students.

Name: Soldiers’ Memorial & Municipal Auditorium Building (Riverside Municipal Auditorium)
Description: Dedicated in 1929 as a memorial to Riverside residents who died in World War I, the Municipal Auditorium was designed as a major civic gathering place for the growing city. Its architecture combines Mission Revival and Moorish influences and includes a large auditorium, arcaded passages and landscaped grounds. Now known as the Riverside Municipal Auditorium, the building has hosted public ceremonies, concerts, performances and community events for nearly a century.

Name: Riverside Art Museum — Former YWCA
Description: Designed by architect Julia Morgan and completed in 1929 for Riverside’s Young Women’s Christian Association, this Spanish Colonial Revival building originally provided meeting rooms, recreation facilities and an indoor swimming pool for women and girls. The Riverside Art Association acquired the building in the 1960s and adapted it as the Riverside Art Museum. It is significant both for its civic and social history and as one of Riverside’s important works by a nationally prominent architect.

Name: Riverside Chinatown Site
Description: Riverside’s principal Chinatown developed here beginning in 1885 after Chinese residents and businesses relocated from an earlier settlement near downtown. The community included stores, residences, boarding houses, a temple and other buildings centered along a street historically known as Mongol Street. Although its last surviving building was demolished in 1978, archaeological investigations beginning in the 1980s demonstrated the site’s exceptional ability to document Chinese immigrant life and the indispensable role Chinese workers played in Riverside’s early agricultural and commercial development.

Name: Fred Stebler House
Description: Built in 1911 for inventor and manufacturer Fred Stebler, this Craftsman-era residence was designed by H. L. Evans. Stebler was a pioneer in the development of machinery for grading, cleaning and packing citrus fruit, helping mechanize an industry central to Riverside’s economy. The house, where Stebler lived until his death in 1957, is notable both for its architecture and for its association with one of Riverside’s important agricultural inventors.

Name: Loring Building
Description: Completed in 1890, the Loring Building was designed by A. C. Willard in the Richardsonian Romanesque style as part of a complex that included the adjoining Loring Opera House. For its first decades it housed Riverside’s City Hall, municipal courts and public library as well as commercial tenants. The exterior was remodeled in 1918 to harmonize with the Mission Revival character developing around the Mission Inn. The adjoining opera house was destroyed by fire in 1990.

Name: New Jerusalem Church
Description: Dedicated on Easter Sunday, April 17, 1904, the New Jerusalem Church is a distinctive late example of Classical Revival church architecture enriched with Gothic elements. Its temple-like façade reflects the architectural eclecticism of turn-of-the-century Riverside. The church was completed during the long ministry of the Rev. Berry Edmiston, who served its congregation from 1885 to 1911.

Name: Harada House
Description: Japanese immigrants Jukichi and Ken Harada purchased this modest house in 1915 in the names of their American-born children because California’s Alien Land Law prohibited Japanese immigrants from owning property. The resulting court case, People v. Harada, ended in 1918 with a Riverside judge affirming the children’s constitutional right to own the home. The case became an important early civil-rights precedent, and Harada House is now recognized as a Riverside City Landmark, California Historical Landmark and National Historic Landmark.

Name: Gage Canal
Description: Constructed under the direction of Matthew Gage beginning in 1884, the Gage Canal carried water from the Santa Ana River across Riverside to Gage’s lands in Arlington Heights. Extended to roughly twenty miles by 1888, the canal made thousands of additional acres available for irrigated agriculture and helped fuel Riverside’s great citrus and real-estate boom of the 1890s. Later lined with concrete and repeatedly improved, it remains one of Riverside’s most important surviving works of nineteenth-century engineering.

Name: “Edgewild”
Description: Built in 1891 for brothers William and Edward Gulick, Edgewild originally stood within their forty-acre citrus ranch and nursery. The large New England-influenced residence recalls the prosperous agricultural estates that once characterized the Hawarden Hills area. After Leroy and Margaret Austin acquired the property in 1922, they extensively improved the house and grounds; their gardens received national recognition in the 1930s.

Name: Mount Rubidoux
Description: Rising immediately west of downtown, Mount Rubidoux became one of Riverside’s defining civic landscapes after Frank A. Miller and his associates acquired the mountain in 1906 and developed a scenic road to its summit. The first Easter Sunrise Service was held here in 1909, beginning a tradition that inspired similar observances nationwide. Among the mountain’s many monuments are the summit cross and Arthur B. Benton’s 1925 Peace Tower and Friendship Bridge. Miller’s heirs donated the mountain to the City in 1955.

Name: John W. North Park
Description: This small park marks the site where John Wesley North, principal founder of Riverside, maintained his home from 1871 to 1880 during the formative years of the new colony. North helped organize the Southern California Colony Association and played a central role in establishing Riverside as a planned community. The property became a City park in 1927, preserving a tangible association with Riverside’s founding.

Name: Former City Hall (Tilden-Coil Constructors)
Description: Completed in 1924, this Spanish Renaissance Revival building was Riverside’s first municipally owned City Hall. Its construction followed voter approval of a 1923 bond issue and provided permanent quarters for a city government that had previously occupied leased space. It remained Riverside’s governmental center until the present City Hall opened in 1975. The historic building was restored for private office use in the 1980s.

Name: “Rockledge”
Description: Built in 1891 for citrus grower and developer Priestley Hall and his wife, Agnes Overton Hall, Rockledge occupies a prominent site overlooking the entrance to the Arlington Heights development. Hall, himself a designer and builder, constructed the imposing Victorian-era residence largely of thick adobe brick manufactured on the property. Its hilltop location was deliberately chosen to create an impressive architectural gateway to the newly developing citrus district beyond Victoria Avenue.

Name: Devine House
Description: Architect John C. Pelton Jr. designed this Queen Anne residence in 1888 for Frank B. and Vinie Devine. Frank Devine was a pioneer of Riverside’s fruit-packing industry, shipping oranges, raisins, dried fruit and honey under the “Sunbeam” label. Built during Riverside’s first great period of citrus prosperity, the elaborate two-story house survives as an important example of the substantial residences constructed by the city’s successful agricultural entrepreneurs.

Name: “Raeburn”
Description: Built in 1897 for William Irving, president of the Gage Canal Company, Raeburn is an imposing Queen Anne residence set within Riverside’s historic citrus greenbelt. Described by the City as the area’s first “grove mansion,” the house reflects the wealth generated by the irrigation and citrus industries that transformed Arlington Heights during the late nineteenth century.

Name: Arcade Building
Description: Designed by prominent Los Angeles architects Walker & Eisen, the Arcade Building was constructed about 1928 for the Security Title Insurance and Guaranty Company. Its Spanish Renaissance design incorporates an interior pedestrian arcade, combining commercial space with the romantic Mediterranean architecture then reshaping downtown Riverside. The building was restored in 1976.

Name: Bonnett Building
Description: Built in 1908, the Bonnett Building is an unusual example of a downtown commercial structure physically altered in response to a changing streetscape. When Orange Street was widened in 1929, owner E. M. Bonnett reconstructed the ground floor at the new property line, using a series of arches to support the projecting second story. The resulting façade gives the building its distinctive Spanish Colonial Revival character.

Name: Estudillo House
Description: Built in 1911 from plans by Riverside architect Seeley L. Pillar, the Estudillo House is a well-preserved California bungalow associated with one of Riverside’s prominent early public officials. Miguel Estudillo, who served in the California Assembly and Senate and for many years as Riverside City Attorney, lived here with his family from 1918 until his death in 1950.

Name: Irvine House
Description: Los Angeles architects Seehorn & Preston designed this distinctive residence in 1906 for Len and Stella Irvine. Its eclectic design combines several architectural influences, including pronounced Norman elements, rather than adhering to a single revival style. Stella Irvine was a prominent temperance advocate who served as regional president of the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union.

Name: Waite House
Description: Construction of this elaborate Queen Anne residence began in 1884 for Riverside pioneers Lyman and Lillian Waite and was completed in its expanded form in 1890. With its towers, steep roofs and richly detailed exterior, the house is one of the city’s notable surviving Victorian-era residences. Lyman Waite served as Riverside’s first notary public and as a local Justice of the Peace.

Name: Cressman House
Description: Designed in 1902 by architects Burnham & Bliesner, the Cressman House is a residential interpretation of the Mission Revival style that was becoming closely associated with Riverside at the turn of the twentieth century. Its original owner, Cressman, worked as a deputy with the Riverside County Sheriff’s Office. The house also reflects the growing popularity of regionally inspired architecture beyond Riverside’s major civic and commercial buildings.

Name: Grant School
Description: Designed by Riverside architect G. Stanley Wilson, Grant School opened in 1935 after the original 1889 school building was demolished following damage from the 1933 Long Beach earthquake. The Mission Revival campus continued a style strongly associated with Riverside’s civic architecture. A fountain installed in 1896 survives from the earlier school grounds, providing a tangible link between the two generations of buildings on the site.

Name: Fox Theater
Description: Designed by the architectural firm Balch & Stanbery, the Fox Theater opened in 1929 as a Spanish Colonial Revival movie and vaudeville palace. Its stage hosted performers including Bing Crosby and Judy Garland, while its proximity to Hollywood made it an important preview theater for motion pictures. In 1939, the Fox hosted the first public screening of Gone with the Wind. Restored by the City, it now operates as the Fox Performing Arts Center.

Name: Seventh Street Historic District
Description: Extending along present-day Mission Inn Avenue from the railroad district toward the Buena Vista Bridge, the Seventh Street Historic District preserves one of Riverside’s most important historic corridors. Developed primarily from the late nineteenth century through the 1930s and ’40s, it contains notable residential, commercial and civic architecture as well as Raincross streetlights and historic streetscape features. The former Seventh Street served as Riverside’s principal east-west gateway between its railroad, citrus-packing and downtown districts.

Name: Former YMCA Building (Life Arts Center)
Description: Built in 1909 as Riverside’s second YMCA building, this Italian Renaissance palazzo–inspired structure served the organization until 1968. In addition to recreational facilities, the building included guest rooms and other spaces intended to support the YMCA’s educational and social mission. It later became the Life Arts Center, continuing its long history as a community-oriented building.

Name: “Greystones”
Description: Built in 1902 for John Mylne, a Canadian immigrant and assistant engineer on the Gage Canal, Greystones is a Classical Revival residence set amid the historic citrus landscape of Hawarden Hills. Its name comes from the locally quarried granite used for the foundation and for retaining walls along the garden and drive. The house reflects both Riverside’s citrus-era prosperity and the development of substantial country residences in Arlington Heights.

Name: Lerner Building
Description: Constructed in 1927 for Moses H. Lerner, the Lerner Building was designed by Joseph R. Scheneck as a brick Italian Renaissance commercial and office building. Its scale and architectural treatment reflect downtown Riverside’s rapid commercial growth during the 1920s, when increasingly substantial office and retail buildings reshaped the city center.

Name: Hole Mansion
Description: Designed by Arthur B. Benton and built between 1912 and 1915 for developer Willits J. Hole, this rustic bungalow was the principal residence of Hole’s extensive La Sierra ranch. Hole had acquired approximately 10,000 acres of the former Rancho La Sierra Sepulveda in 1909. Constructed with massive local-stone walls and set within landscaped grounds, the house survives as an important reminder of La Sierra’s ranching and agricultural period before suburban development.

Name: Collins-Seaton House
Description: Los Angeles architect O. P. Dennis designed this Classical Revival residence in 1900 for real-estate broker William S. Collins and his wife. Banker George A. Seaton acquired the house in 1902 and installed much of its elaborate interior woodwork, while the residence became a setting for Riverside social events. Its prominent classical composition and surviving porte-cochère make it one of the city’s strongest examples of turn-of-the-century Classical Revival residential architecture.

Name: Arlington Branch Library
Description: Designed by Riverside architect Seeley L. Pillar and completed in 1909, the Arlington Branch Library is Riverside’s oldest surviving library building and its first purpose-built branch library. Funded in part by philanthropist Andrew Carnegie, the Classical Revival building served not only as a library but at various times also accommodated the fire department, National Guard and Depression-era relief services. G. Stanley Wilson designed a 1927–28 remodeling.

Name: Batkin-Chrysler House
Description: Built in 1896 for John S. Batkin, the Batkin-Chrysler House is a substantial Queen Anne residence characteristic of Riverside’s late nineteenth-century prosperity. Its irregular massing, detailed exterior and spacious interior reflect the elaborate domestic architecture favored by successful Riverside residents during the citrus boom. The house has remained one of the city’s notable surviving Victorian-era residences.

Name: Riverside City College Quadrangle
Description: Begun in 1924 from designs by Riverside architect G. Stanley Wilson, the Riverside City College Quadrangle developed in stages around a central courtyard, recalling the organization and appearance of an Italian Renaissance palazzo. The first buildings provided dedicated facilities for the young Riverside Junior College, which until then had shared space with Riverside Polytechnic High School. Additional wings, including the auditorium, gradually completed the complex during the 1920s and early 1930s.

Name: Former University Heights Junior High School (César Chávez Community Center)
Description: Designed by John C. Austin of the Los Angeles firm Austin & Ashley, University Heights Junior High School opened in 1928 as an imposing Spanish Colonial Revival campus. Its opening coincided with the end of gender-segregated junior-high instruction in Riverside. After the school closed in 1972, the City acquired the property for community use; the main building now serves as the César Chávez Community Center at Bobby Bonds Park. It is also listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

Name: Former Rouse’s Department Store Building (UCR Arts)
Description: Originally built in 1895, this Main Street commercial building was remodeled several times as Rouse’s grew into one of downtown Riverside’s leading department stores. Its most important transformation came in 1924, when architect G. Stanley Wilson redesigned the façade with details inspired by fifteenth-century Spanish Renaissance architecture. Portions of Wilson’s work survive on the upper story, preserving the building’s association with Riverside’s early twentieth-century retail district.

Name: Ward House
Description: Built in 1887 by undertaker George F. Ward for his family, the Ward House is a well-preserved Victorian residence incorporating Queen Anne and Eastlake details. Ward was also active in civic life, serving as chief of Riverside’s volunteer fire department from 1890 to 1896 and later as a member of the City Council. The house survives as an important example of Riverside’s late nineteenth-century residential architecture.

Name: Peter J. Weber House
Description: This house was designed and built by architect Peter J. Weber in the 1930s as a family residence and an expression of his creative work. The house is notable for its eclectic Depression-era design inspired by Medieval Spanish brick and half-timbering structures (with additional elements of Moorish and broadly Mediterranean influences), its reliance on salvaged materials, and its thoughtful energy-conserving systems.

Name: Moulton House
Description: Built in 1899 for Ernest and Julia Moulton, this substantial Classical Revival residence reflects the prosperity of Riverside at the height of its citrus-era development. Ernest Moulton was a prominent local businessman who served as president of the First National Bank of Riverside. The house is one of the surviving large residences that once gave Magnolia Avenue much of its distinguished residential character.

Name: Victoria Bridge
Description: The first Victoria Bridge was constructed of wood in 1891 to connect the newly developing Arlington Heights tract with central Riverside. It later carried a streetcar line but proved inadequate for increasingly heavy traffic. The present reinforced-concrete bridge, completed in 1928 and designed by engineer R. V. Leeson, replaced the earlier structure while maintaining this important link along historic Victoria Avenue.

Name: Hoover House
Description: Citrus grower and Riverside County Supervisor Martin Hoover and his wife built this residence in 1908, combining elements of the Queen Anne and Classical Revival styles. Originally located on Seventh Street, the house was moved to Redwood Drive rather than demolished, becoming the first Riverside building relocated specifically as part of the City’s historic-preservation efforts. Its preservation marked an important early milestone in Riverside’s developing commitment to historic conservation.

Name: Former Palm School (Riverside Adult School)
Description: Designed by Riverside architect G. Stanley Wilson and completed in 1927, Palm Elementary School is a Spanish Colonial Revival campus characteristic of Wilson’s civic work during the period. It served generations of Riverside students before closing as a conventional elementary school in the 1970s and later housed Riverside Unified School District programs. Its architecture reflects the widespread use of Spanish and Mission-inspired forms in Riverside’s early twentieth-century public buildings.

Name: White Park
Description: Established in 1883, White Park is Riverside’s oldest city park. Early improvements transformed the site into a lush botanical garden with ornamental plantings, a bandstand, footbridges and a canal, creating an important recreational landscape in the growing city. Although the park has changed substantially over time, it remains one of Riverside’s earliest surviving public spaces and an important remnant of nineteenth-century civic planning.

Name: Orchard House
Description: Constructed between 1917 and 1920 for attorney and citrus grower William G. Irving, Orchard House is a large Tudor Revival residence set within the historic citrus landscape of Hawarden Hills. Its twelve-room design reflects the estate-scale homes developed among Riverside’s prosperous agricultural and professional families during the early twentieth century. The surrounding setting preserves a strong connection to the area’s citrus-growing past.

Name: “La Ventanilla” Robert Bettner House
Description: Built in 1892 for Robert and Lucy Bettner, this picturesque single-story residence is one of the few surviving houses from the period when Magnolia Avenue was lined with elegant homes and citrus estates. The Bettners called the house “La Ventanilla,” or “the house of little windows.” Robert Bettner, a member of one of Riverside’s prominent citrus families, later entered the real-estate business. The house and its landscaped grounds preserve an increasingly rare glimpse of nineteenth-century Magnolia Avenue.

Name: Chicago White Sox Redwood Tree
Description: This coast redwood was planted in 1914 during a visit to Riverside by members of the Chicago White Sox baseball team, commemorating the city’s connection with professional baseball and spring exhibition games. Team owner Charles A. Comiskey later provided a commemorative tablet for the tree. More than a century later, the redwood survives in Low Park as an unusual living landmark linking Riverside’s landscape history with the early years of Major League Baseball.

Name: Montezuma Bald Cypress Trees
Description: These Montezuma bald cypress trees are among the oldest surviving landscape features at Fairmount Park. Their planting is generally attributed to Captain Charles Dexter, one of the park’s founders, around 1903. The trees were later incorporated into the expanded lake landscape and survived major alterations to the park, including the 1938 flood. They remain a distinctive living reminder of Fairmount Park’s earliest development.

Name: Magnolia Avenue Parkways & Center Median
Description: This landscaped section of Magnolia Avenue preserves the character of one of Riverside’s earliest and most influential scenic boulevards. Beginning in 1876, eucalyptus, oaks, palms and other plantings were used to create a broad, park-like avenue through the growing community. Its combination of roadway, landscaped median and parkways helped establish a model for ornamental urban streetscapes and remains an important part of Riverside’s historic landscape identity.

Name: Palm Grove
Description: This collection of thirty-four palms represents six varieties and was moved to Hunter Park in 1962 from the former Harrison Wright residence near Adams Street and Magnolia Avenue. Preserved together rather than dispersed or removed, the grove reflects Riverside’s long horticultural tradition and the importance of palms to the city’s historic landscape character.

Name: Roosevelt Palm
Description: President Theodore Roosevelt planted this Mexican fan palm on May 8, 1903, during his visit to Riverside. Originally known as the Queen Victoria Palm, the tree became a living memorial to Roosevelt’s visit and to Riverside’s prominence during the height of the citrus era. It remains one of the city’s most directly documented historic trees and is prominently located along Victoria Avenue.

Name: Native Sycamore Tree
Description: This mature native sycamore marks the former site of the Lee Duncan Ranch, where Duncan trained and cared for the famous motion-picture dog Rin-Tin-Tin. Preserved within a residential median, the tree is significant less for its horticultural rarity than for its association with one of Riverside’s unusual connections to early Hollywood history.

Name: Horse Chestnut Tree
Description: Local horticulturist Captain Damner originally planted this horse chestnut at his home near Mary Street and Victoria Avenue. When Mary Street was widened in 1978, the City transplanted the mature tree into the center divider of Victoria Avenue rather than remove it. Its preservation reflects both Riverside’s horticultural heritage and the City’s early recognition that significant landscape features could merit the same protection as historic buildings.

Name: Evergreen Cemetery & Riverside Mausoleum
Description: Established in 1872, Evergreen is Riverside’s oldest cemetery and the burial place of many people central to the city’s history, including John W. North, Frank A. Miller, and Luther and Eliza Tibbets. The Egyptian Revival mausoleum was built in 1914 by W. C. Crowell of Pasadena. Together, the cemetery and mausoleum form an exceptionally important historic landscape documenting Riverside’s founding generation and subsequent civic development.

Name: Mitchell House
Description: Built in 1893 for David G. Mitchell, this two-story Queen Anne residence was one of four Riverside houses constructed from the same stock plan. Mitchell, a Civil War veteran who fought at Gettysburg, helped organize the movement that created Riverside County and was elected county treasurer in its first election in 1893. He and his family lived here until 1907.

Name: Fairmount Park
Description: Fairmount Park developed from the late nineteenth century into Riverside’s principal municipal recreation landscape. In 1911, the nationally prominent Olmsted Brothers prepared a plan for the park, influencing its arrangement of open lawns, lakes, circulation and planted areas. Subsequent additions created the landscape familiar today, including Lake Evans, recreational facilities and civic gathering spaces. The park remains one of Riverside’s most important historic public landscapes.

Name: “Harwood Hall”
Description: Built in 1904 for Harwood Hall, the first superintendent of the Sherman Institute, this one-and-a-half-story residence is an excellent example of the California bungalow. Hall oversaw the federal Indian boarding school during its early years, making the house significant not only architecturally but also for its association with the administration of a federal institution created as part of the broader assimilationist boarding-school system imposed on Native American students.

Name: Shiels House
Description: Built in 1887 by G. Olivo Newman, the Shiels House is a late Victorian residence in Prospect Place, one of Riverside’s earliest residential subdivisions. John Shiels and his family first rented the house in 1901, purchased it in 1906, and continued to occupy it for more than six decades. The house preserves an important link to Riverside’s early neighborhood development outside the original downtown core.

Name: McIntyre House
Description: Built about 1892 by Riverside designer-builder D. J. McLeod for attorney William J. McIntyre, this residence is a highly intact example of Victorian architecture with strong Eastlake influence. McIntyre served as Riverside City Attorney and was active in the movement that led to the creation of Riverside County. Long ownership by only two families helped preserve much of the house’s original character.

Name: Newman Park and the De Anza Statue
Description: Created in 1940 with support from the Works Progress Administration, the De Anza monument commemorates Spanish explorer Juan Bautista de Anza. Artist Dorr Bothwell designed the work and Sherry Peticolas sculpted it, using Ed J. Loustanau, a descendant of De Anza’s brother, as the model. Set within Newman Park, the sculpture is a notable example of Riverside’s Depression-era public art.

Name: Buena Vista Bridge
Description: Completed in 1931 as part of improvements to Riverside’s western gateway, Buena Vista Bridge was designed by Davidson and Fulmor and constructed with locally quarried, hand-cut stone. Its picturesque design complemented the widening of the Santa Ana River bridge and the former Seventh Street approach to downtown. The bridge remains a distinctive component of the historic entrance to Riverside at the foot of Mount Rubidoux.

Name: Stone House, 3241 Mary Street
Description: Built in 1929, this modest residence is one of Riverside’s best surviving examples of the vernacular stone houses and bungalows constructed in the region during the 1910s and 1920s. Its use of exposed local stone reflects a building tradition that combined inexpensive native materials with the informal scale and craftsmanship associated with California bungalow architecture.

Name: Stone House, 2110 Mission Inn Avenue
Description: Constructed in 1926, this residence is another important example of Riverside’s vernacular stone-building tradition. Its walls of local stone and modest bungalow form typify a once more common regional construction method of the early twentieth century. The house also contributes to the historic character of the Seventh Street East Historic District, where the City identifies it as one of the area’s notable landmarks.

Name: Hammer-Wallihan House
Description: Designed by Riverside architect Henry L. A. Jekel and built in 1926, the Hammer-Wallihan House is a particularly refined example of the city’s stone bungalow tradition. Jekel adapted the rustic qualities of local stone construction to a carefully composed residential design, combining craftsmanship and picturesque massing with the informal character associated with Southern California bungalow architecture.

Name: Jarvis House
Description: Built in 1888 for John T. Jarvis, this substantial Victorian residence was dramatically remodeled in 1914 to reflect changing architectural tastes. Its original tower and third-story dormers were removed, while a broad porch and central gable gave the house a more bungalow-like appearance. Jarvis was a prominent Riverside businessman and civic leader who served on the City Council and later as mayor.

Name: William Collier House
Description: Built for Riverside attorney William Collier around 1892, this Queen Anne residence is associated with a prominent early lawyer and developer who helped establish the communities of Lake Elsinore and Wildomar. R. H. Polkinghorn, later Riverside County’s first County Administrator, subsequently occupied the house. Threatened with demolition, it was moved from Prospect Avenue to its present location on Lime Street in 1987.

Name: M. H. Simons Undertaking Chapel
Description: Designed by G. Stanley Wilson and completed in 1925 for mortician Melvin H. Simons, this Mission Revival building was purpose-built to accommodate the specialized requirements of an undertaking business. Its architecture represents some of Wilson’s strongest commercial work and reflects the 1920s civic effort to give downtown Riverside a cohesive Mission and Spanish Colonial architectural identity. The Simons family operated the mortuary here until 1966.

Name: William Childs House
Description: Built in 1910, the William Childs House is a Craftsman bungalow associated with the former 200-acre Monte Vista Nursery. Childs was a partner in the nursery, which specialized in oranges, and the house survives as a residential reminder of the extensive citrus-growing and nursery operations that once occupied this part of Riverside.

Name: “Hartree Grove”
Description: Hartree Grove began as an adobe residence constructed in 1892. Its second owner, Herman Wilson, acquired the property in 1899 and named it after a family castle in Scotland. In 1901 he remodeled the house to resemble a Scottish country house, giving the property the distinctive appearance it retains today.

Name: First Christian Church Parsonage
Description: Built in the 1880s as the parsonage for Riverside’s First Christian Church, this early residence originally stood at 3737 Vine Street. It was moved to its present location on Mission Inn Avenue in 1993 and adapted for use as a private residence. Its preservation records both Riverside’s early religious history and the city’s practice of relocating threatened historic buildings.

Name: Former Aurea Vista Hotel (Aurea Vista Nightclub)
Description: Designed by Riverside architect G. Stanley Wilson and completed in 1927, the Aurea Vista Hotel is a Spanish-Moorish style building created primarily for long-term residential guests. Its richly styled exterior reflects the popularity of Spanish and Mediterranean revival architecture in Riverside during the 1920s and Wilson’s important role in shaping the city’s architectural character.

Name: Former Casa de Anza Motel (Santa Cruz Inn)
Description: Casa de Anza developed around an earlier duplex that was moved to the site about 1923. In 1939, architect G. Stanley Wilson designed the Spanish Colonial Revival motel complex that incorporated the older building. The property reflects the rise of automobile tourism and roadside lodging in Riverside during the early twentieth century.

Name: Rockledge Cottage
Description: Built in 1901 as a one-story Craftsman residence for Englishman Hugh G. Newton, Rockledge Cottage was enlarged around 1910 with a second story designed by architect Franklin P. Burnham, designer of the Riverside County Courthouse. New York banker William A. Lombard purchased the property in 1917 and gave it the name Rockledge Cottage.

Name: Tetley Building
Description: Architect G. Stanley Wilson designed this Spanish Colonial style commercial complex for Riverside businessman Frank A. Tetley, with construction beginning in 1925. The buildings reflect the coordinated Spanish and Mediterranean architectural character that increasingly defined Riverside’s commercial districts during the 1920s.

Name: Henry M. Streeter House
Description: Designed and built by Henry A. Westbrook in 1888, this Victorian farmhouse was constructed for Henry M. Streeter, a prominent Riverside attorney and politician. Streeter served in both the California Assembly and Senate and authored the legislation that created Riverside County in 1893. The house is significant both for its architecture and for its association with one of the county’s principal founders.

Name: James M. Wood House
Description: Built in 1891, this Colonial Revival residence was designed for theatrical architect James M. Wood in collaboration with Riverside architect A. C. Willard. Wood had come to Riverside to design the interior of the Loring Opera House, while Willard designed that building’s exterior. The house preserves an unusual residential connection between two architects associated with one of Riverside’s most important lost entertainment buildings.

Name: Roosevelt Building
Description: Designed by Burnham & Bliesner and constructed by Fred Peter in 1904, the Roosevelt Building is an Italianate commercial building in downtown Riverside. It was named for President Theodore Roosevelt, whose 1903 visit to Riverside was commemorated in several places around the city. The building remains a substantial example of Riverside’s early twentieth-century commercial architecture.

Name: “Ridgecourt”
Description: Built in 1913 for Clinton Hickok, a piano dealer from Toledo, Ohio, Ridgecourt is a Mission Revival residence with an especially whimsical feature: its patio was designed in the shape of a grand piano. The house reflects the popularity of Mission-inspired residential architecture in Riverside during the early twentieth century.

Name: J. R. Willis Building
Description: Designed by G. Stanley Wilson in 1927 for the Bell Cleaning Company, this Spanish Colonial Revival commercial building reflects Riverside’s strong preference for Spanish and Mediterranean architectural forms during the 1920s. Originally built for a dry-cleaning business, it is one of Wilson’s surviving contributions to the city’s commercial streetscape.

Name: John J. Hewitt House
Description: John and Martha Hewitt built this Eastlake Victorian residence in 1885 on their ten-acre orange grove. After John Hewitt’s death in 1909, Martha subdivided the property into forty-three residential lots and had the house cut into two sections, rotated ninety degrees and moved to face Orange Street. She continued to live there until 1920.

Name: Dr. Edmund Jaeger House
Description: This property is no longer a designated City Landmark. Dr. Edmund Jaeger, a Riverside City College biology instructor and noted desert naturalist, designed its front garden as a carefully composed collection of desert plants selected for texture, form, color and succession of bloom. Because the garden was the principal basis for designation and no longer survives, the property was removed from the landmark list.

Name: First United Brethren in Christ
Description: Built in 1887, this Gothic Revival church is identified by the City as Riverside’s second-oldest surviving church building. Its steeply pitched form and pointed-arch detailing preserve an important example of the modest ecclesiastical architecture constructed during Riverside’s early development.

Name: Former Irving School (Abraham Lincoln High School)
Description: The surviving Craftsman-style school building was constructed in 1917. A Streamline Moderne auditorium designed by G. Stanley Wilson was added in 1940. The campus once contained nine buildings, but a 1955 fire destroyed the others, leaving these structures as the principal remnants of the historic school.

Name: Chudzikowski Home Site
Description: This property formerly contained a residence, garage and entrance monument constructed for John B. Chudzikowski. All of the designated improvements were demolished in 1999, leaving the site as a landmark associated primarily with the history of the lost property rather than surviving architecture.

Name: Former Potter Hotel (White Park Building)
Description: Built in 1924 by Walter Lewis at a reported cost of $15,000, the White Park Building is a Mediterranean-style commercial structure facing Riverside’s historic White Park. Its design reflects the Spanish and Mediterranean architectural vocabulary that became increasingly common in Riverside commercial development during the 1920s.

Name: Benjamin Rockhold Family House
Description: Built in 1906, this distinctive residence combines Swiss Chalet and Craftsman influences. The house originally stood at 4220 Lemon Street and was moved to Indian Hill Road in 1998. Benjamin Rockhold and his brother John established the Rockhold Brothers Grocery in 1889, linking the house to one of Riverside’s early commercial families.

Name: Santa Fe Depot
Description: Built in the 1920s for the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway, this Pueblo Revival depot replaced an earlier Victorian station on the same site. The City’s landmark plaque credits C. S. Gilman and M. R. Mohr of Los Angeles with its design. Its massed stucco walls and Southwestern forms reflect the architectural identity adopted by the Santa Fe across the region. Scheduled passenger service ended in 1968.

Name: Elmer A. Day House
Description: Built in 1895 for horticulturist Elmer A. Day, this Vernacular Victorian residence originally stood on Eighth Street, now University Avenue, amid citrus groves. As downtown Riverside became increasingly commercial, the house was moved to its present Fourth Street location in 1911. Its relocation reflects the transition of central Riverside from an agricultural settlement into a growing commercial city.

Name: Former Food Manufacturing Corporation Building
Description: Constructed between 1938 and 1943, this group of industrial buildings was designed with distinctive sawtooth roofs oriented north to provide even, diffused natural light. The complex is associated with the Food Manufacturing Corporation, later part of FMC, and represents Riverside’s twentieth-century industrial development alongside the citrus packing and agricultural industries that shaped the city’s economy.

Name: Jaeger Family House
Description: Built in 1907 by G. D. Haigh for the Jaeger family, this Craftsman residence dates from a period of rapid residential development west of Riverside’s original Mile Square. The family had moved from Des Moines, Iowa, the previous year. Their son, Dr. Edmund C. Jaeger, lived here for many years and became an internationally recognized naturalist, educator and authority on the flora and fauna of the desert Southwest.

Name: Raymond Cree–Criddle House
Description: Built in 1913, this Craftsman bungalow is an important contributor to the Mount Rubidoux Historic District and was home to several prominent Riverside residents. Original owner Raymond Cree served as Riverside County Superintendent of Schools. Later owner Eugene B. Criddle was vice president of the Southern Sierras Power Company and served as mayor of Riverside from 1933 to 1937.

Name: “St. Valentine Hall” Mary & Emerson Holt House
Description: Built in 1924, this Spanish Colonial Revival residence was home to Emerson and Mary Holt, both active in Riverside civic life. Emerson was a businessman, Masonic chaplain and co-founder of Riverside’s Sierra Club chapter. Mary was a writer, artist and women’s-club leader who wrote the lyrics to the Riverside County Song. The house is an important contributor to the Wood Streets Historic District.

Name: Alkire House
Description: Built about 1899 by Adam S. Alkire, this Neoclassical residence is associated with one of Riverside’s early civic figures and with the development of the city’s original Mile Square. Alkire, a Civil War veteran, merchant, photographer and public official, served as Riverside’s City Clerk and Assessor and later developed several properties along Orange Street. The house also contributes to the Heritage Square Historic District.

Name: Holden House
Description: In 1923, Arthur and Virginia Holden commissioned Riverside architect Robert H. Spurgeon to design this Tudor Revival residence on Magnolia Avenue. Arthur Holden had come to Riverside in 1907 to manage the British-owned San Jacinto Land Company, which controlled extensive acreage in the region. The house is a substantial example of the picturesque revival-style residences built along Magnolia Avenue during the early twentieth century.

Name: Ames–Westbrook House
Description: Built in 1888 for citrus grower Samuel A. Ames, this Queen Anne residence is one of Riverside’s notable surviving Victorian houses. It is most closely associated with longtime owners John R. and Lucie Westbrook. John Westbrook helped establish Franzen Brothers Hardware, which later became the J. R. Westbrook Company. The house retains much of the elaborate form and decorative character typical of late nineteenth-century Queen Anne architecture.

Name: Highgrove Drop & Upper Riverside Canal
Description: The Upper Riverside Canal is closely associated with the development of Riverside’s irrigation system and citrus industry. At the Highgrove Drop, where the canal descended approximately forty feet near Iowa Avenue, engineers harnessed the falling water to create one of California’s earliest commercially significant hydroelectric plants. Beginning in 1888, its generators supplied electricity for street lighting in Riverside and Colton, linking this site to both the city’s agricultural and electrical history.

Name: Piddington House
Description: Designed by architect Henry L. A. Jekel and built in 1927 by John V. Philbrick for Alfred A. and Erminie Piddington, this Spanish Colonial Revival residence stands in the Fairmount Heights subdivision overlooking Riverside’s historic North Hill quarry. Alfred Piddington worked for the Riverside Press and Enterprise for forty-six years and became the newspaper’s editor in 1933. The house is an important example of Jekel’s residential work in Riverside.

Name: Lillian M. Spurgeon Residence
Description: Designed in 1927 by architect Robert H. Spurgeon for his mother, Lillian M. Spurgeon, this Spanish Colonial Revival residence is an excellent example of the style’s adaptation to domestic architecture in Riverside. Spurgeon practiced in New York, Los Angeles, Riverside and Santa Barbara, with much of his career centered in Riverside. The house is notable both for its architectural quality and for its association with one of the city’s important twentieth-century architects.

Name: R. D. Brough–Harry W. Hammond Residence
Description: Constructed in 1908, this Craftsman residence is significant both for its architecture and for its association with Harry W. Hammond, a longtime principal of the Riverside Press. Hammond lived here for seventeen years during a forty-nine-year career with the newspaper. The house is a strong example of the Craftsman style that became popular in Riverside during the early twentieth century.

Name: John Swanson Residence
Description: Built by John Swanson about 1906, this residence is an unusual example of transitional architecture in Riverside. Its design combines Victorian, Classical Revival and Arts and Crafts influences, illustrating the changing architectural tastes of the early twentieth century. The Cultural Heritage Board identified it as one of the city’s most distinctive surviving examples of this stylistic transition.

Name: Jackson Building
Description: Constructed about 1886, the Jackson Building became an important center of Riverside’s Japanese immigrant community. Its upper floor contained largely Japanese lodgings, while shops and businesses operated below, including the Japanese-owned Washington Restaurant. Jukichi Harada became proprietor of the restaurant in 1911, several years before his family’s landmark challenge to California’s Alien Land Law. The building preserves an important association with Riverside’s Japanese American history.

Name: Ernest & Louise Clarke House
Description: Henry L. A. Jekel designed this Spanish Colonial Revival residence for Ernest and Louise Clarke in 1928. Ernest Clarke served for decades as editor of the Riverside Daily Press and later headed the combined Press-Enterprise. Dr. Louise Harvey Clarke was the first woman president of the Riverside County Medical Association and the only woman physician among the sixteen founders of Riverside Community Hospital. The house is significant for both its Jekel design and its association with two prominent Riverside residents.

Name: C. O. Evans House
Description: Designed and built in 1908 by Riverside architect G. Stanley Wilson for Charles Orrick Evans and his family, this residence combines California bungalow forms with Tudor influences. Constructed of redwood, brick and concrete, it is an important example of Wilson’s early residential work. Evans was a prominent Riverside businessman and civic figure, adding an important historical association to the house’s architectural significance.

Name: Five Points Intersection
Description: The Five Points intersection became the commercial center of La Sierra during and after World War II, when rapid residential and business development transformed the area. Stores, offices and other services clustered around the meeting of La Sierra Avenue, Pierce Street, Hole Avenue and Bushnell Avenue. Five Points functioned as La Sierra’s historic downtown and as the western gateway to Riverside, La Sierra University and nearby Camp Anza. City planning documents continue to recognize the intersection as City Landmark No. 118.

Name: Walter C. Banks Residence
Description: The Walter C. Banks Residence is a historic dwelling within Riverside’s North Hill area, a neighborhood characterized by early twentieth-century residential development overlooking the city. The house is associated with Walter C. Banks and contributes to the architectural and historical character of this distinctive residential enclave.

Name: All Saints Episcopal Church
Description: Built in 1948, All Saints Episcopal Church is an important example of Mediterranean Revival ecclesiastical architecture and of Riverside’s postwar suburban growth. Its sanctuary is distinguished by extensive board-formed reinforced concrete construction, including carefully formed columns, arches and other architectural details. The City found the church significant for its architecture, craftsmanship, association with a notable designer and its representation of the postwar movement of established downtown congregations into suburban Riverside.

Name: Bobby Bonds Residence
Description: Robert and Elizabeth Bonds moved to this modest Eastside residence in 1957 with their four children. Their son Bobby Bonds became one of Riverside’s most accomplished professional athletes, combining exceptional power and speed during a seventeen-year Major League Baseball career. His sister Rosie competed in the 1964 Olympics, and his son Barry Bonds, born in Riverside while the family lived here, later became one of baseball’s most prominent players. The City designated the property for its association with Riverside-born athletes of national significance.

Name: Jasper Austin Payton Residence
Description: (description tk)

Name: Archibald C. E. Hawthorne House
Description: Built in 1889–90 for Archibald C. E. Hawthorne and designed by architect A. C. Willard, this Swiss Chalet–influenced residence is a rare survivor of the grove houses that once lined Magnolia Avenue. Its broad eaves, decorative braces and unusual cross-shaped plan distinguish the house from Riverside’s more elaborate Victorian residences. The City recognized it as an important remnant of the agricultural residential landscape that characterized areas beyond Riverside’s early town center.

Name: Former Marcy Branch Library
Description: Designed by Riverside architect Herman Ruhnau and completed in 1957, the former Marcy Branch Library reflects Riverside’s rapid postwar growth and the expansion of municipal services into developing neighborhoods. Construction was funded in part by a bequest from Riverside resident Charles F. Marcy. The building is an important local example of Mid-Century Modern civic architecture and was identified by the City as significant for its design, craftsmanship and association with Ruhnau.

Name: Clinton and Geraldine Marr House #2
Description: Architect Clinton Marr designed this Mid-Century Modern residence for his own family in 1960. The post-and-beam house exemplifies the modern residential architecture that developed in Riverside’s Hawarden Hills during the postwar period, emphasizing exposed structural systems and a close relationship between interior spaces and the surrounding landscape. The City designated the property both as an important example of Mid-Century Modern design and for its association with Marr, one of Riverside’s leading twentieth-century architects.

Name: Philip Esbensen House
Description: Architect Philip Esbensen designed this Mid-Century Modern post-and-beam residence for his own family in 1965. Built on a steep hillside, the house uses simple geometric forms, strong horizontal massing, exposed structural elements and expansive floor-to-ceiling glazing to connect its interior with the surrounding landscape. The City identified it as an exceptionally intact example of Riverside’s postwar Modernist residential architecture and one of the city’s last significant examples of the post-and-beam type.

Name: Mackey House
Description: Architect Lois Davidson Gottlieb, a former apprentice of Frank Lloyd Wright, designed the Mackey House in 1967 in collaboration with owners Edward and Barbara Mackey; construction was completed in 1971. The Mid-Century Modern residence is carefully integrated into its rocky hillside site and oriented to views and the movement of the sun. Poured-in-place concrete, clerestory and geometric windows, custom built-in furnishings and repeated chevron motifs give the house a distinctive architectural character.

Name: Trujillo Adobe
Description: Constructed about 1862 by members of the Trujillo family, the Trujillo Adobe predates the founding of Riverside and is considered the city’s oldest surviving structure. The adobe is associated with La Placita de los Trujillos, a settlement established by Spanish-speaking families who migrated from New Mexico to the Santa Ana River valley beginning in the 1840s. Located near the historic Old Spanish Trail, the surviving structure preserves an exceptionally important link to the multicultural settlement of Inland Southern California before Riverside’s establishment in 1870.

Name: Nielsen Pool House
Description: Designed in 1964 by civil and structural engineer Svend Nielsen as his family home and completed in 1966, the Nielsen Pool House is a distinctive example of Mid-Century Modern residential architecture. The semi-subterranean house incorporates strong horizontal lines, ribbon windows, a flat roof and an unusual indoor swimming pool at the center of the design. The City designated the residence for both its architectural character and its association with Nielsen, a prominent structural engineer.

Name: Former Main Library (The Cheech)
Description: Completed during Riverside’s postwar expansion, the former Main Library is an important local example of New Formalism. Its symmetrical composition, broad projecting roofline, brick walls and distinctive patterned concrete screens give the building a monumental but restrained civic character. City historic-resource studies identified the library as eligible for landmark designation for its architecture and its role in Riverside’s twentieth-century civic development.

Name: Gore Manor
Description: Designed by architect Garrett Beekman Van Pelt Jr. and built in 1932 for Thomas E. Gore, Gore Manor is a distinguished Colonial Revival residence. Gore was a prominent Riverside citrus grower, banker and civic leader who promoted the city’s citrus industry and played an important role in developing Riverside’s international relationships, including its sister-city connection with Sendai, Japan. The landmark is significant for both its architecture and its association with Gore.

Name: Farm House Motel
Description: Constructed in 1953, the Farm House Motel is a surviving example of the postwar motor-court motel and California Ranch architecture. Its farmhouse theme is expressed through gambrel roofs, board-and-batten siding, multi-light windows and doors, and a distinctive gambrel-roof-shaped neon pole sign added in 1958. Located along what was then a major highway route, the motel reflects the automobile tourism that once shaped development along University Avenue.

Name: E. T. Wall Packing House #2
Description: Built as part of the E. T. Wall citrus-packing operation, this industrial building represents the large-scale processing and shipping infrastructure that supported Riverside’s citrus economy. Its designation recognizes both the importance of packing houses to the city’s agricultural history and the increasingly rare survival of buildings associated with that once-dominant industry. The City designated the property as Landmark No. 142 in 2020.

Name: Neblett Residence
Description: Designed by Riverside architect Clinton Marr in the mid-1960s for Dr. and Mrs. Edward Neblett, this Mid-Century Modern residence is a notable example of post-and-beam residential architecture in Hawarden Hills. Its low profile, exposed structural expression and close relationship to its landscaped setting reflect the modern residential design that characterized some of Riverside’s most architecturally ambitious postwar neighborhoods.

Name: Powell–Wheeler Residence
Description: Designed by Henry L. A. Jekel and constructed in 1930 for Percy and Margaret Powell, this Monterey Revival residence combines Spanish Colonial influences with the broad balconies and restrained forms associated with the style. Powell was active in Riverside beautification efforts, including projects along Magnolia Avenue. The house was later owned by physician Dr. Omer Wheeler, who served as president of the California Medical Board in the 1950s.

Name: Miné Okubo Residence
Description: Built about 1900, this residence was home to Japanese American artist and author Miné Okubo and her family beginning in 1925. The family purchased the property in 1930 in the name of Okubo’s American-born sibling, an ownership arrangement made legally possible by the 1918 People v. Harada decision. In 1942, Executive Order 9066 forced the Okubo family from Riverside. Miné Okubo later documented her wartime incarceration in the influential 1946 book Citizen 13660.

Name: Mercantile Hall & Orange Valley Masonic Lodge #13
Description: Built and opened in 1905 by David Stokes and other Black investors, Mercantile Hall became an important commercial and social center for Riverside’s African American community. Stokes and Aaron Wiley operated a grocery on the first floor, alongside other businesses, while the upper floor provided meeting space for community organizations and Black fraternal orders, including Orange Valley Masonic Lodge No. 13. Contemporary accounts described the hall as one of Riverside’s most ambitious Black-owned enterprises.

Name: Boyd Residence
Description: Designed in 1957 by architect Charles O. Matcham and completed in 1959 by builder Harry Marsh for Philip and Dorothy Boyd, this Hollywood Regency residence remains remarkably intact. Philip Boyd was a businessman, former mayor of Palm Springs, state legislator and a leading advocate for the establishment of the University of California, Riverside, later serving as a UC Regent. Dorothy Boyd was also active in Riverside civic and charitable organizations. The house is significant for both its architectural character and its association with a couple who played an important role in UCR’s development.

Name: Riverside City Hall
Description: Designed by the Riverside architectural firm Ruhnau, Evans and Steinmann, City Hall represents an unusual blend of Brutalism and New Formalism. Its flat roofs, raised plaza, repetitive geometric forms and curtain wall of arches temper the monumentality of Brutalist design with a more formal civic composition intended to complement nearby landmarks such as the Mission Inn and County Courthouse. The City designated the building for both its architecture and its association with one of Riverside’s most prominent mid-century architectural firms.

Name: Hays-Pattee Residence
Description: Originally designed in 1903 by architect Franklin P. Burnham, the Hays-Pattee Residence began as an Arts and Crafts house with handcrafted detailing and a broad porch supported by substantial stone columns. In 1912, architect Garrett Van Pelt Jr. designed a second-story addition that introduced Mission Revival features including stucco walls, red clay tile roofing and arched windows. The resulting house is a distinctive blend of two important early twentieth-century architectural movements and represents the work of two notable Southern California architects.

Name: “Lionhead”
Description: Designed by Riverside architect Henry L. A. Jekel and built in 1926, Lionhead is a substantial Spanish Eclectic residence set within the historic residential landscape near Victoria Avenue. Its design reflects Jekel’s highly individual interpretation of Spanish and Mediterranean revival architecture during one of the most productive periods of his Riverside career. The property was historically given the name “Lionhead,” which the City retained as part of its landmark designation. City records identify the house as a significant example of Jekel’s residential work and Riverside’s 1920s architectural development.

Name: “Edie”
Description: Designed by Swiss-born architect E. Kurt Steinmann for Dr. Robert R. and Margaret R. Robinson and constructed in 1966–67, Edie is a well-preserved example of Mid-Century Modern residential design. The post-and-beam house features a flat roof, expansive glazing and a strong relationship between its interior spaces and surrounding landscape. The City found the residence significant both as an intact expression of Mid-Century Modern architecture and as a rare surviving Riverside residence by Steinmann, who later contributed to the design of Riverside City Hall and the Main Street pedestrian mall.
